extracted.intended_audience: journalists, public relations professionals, media regulators, and readers interested in media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, practices, ethical concerns, and legal/regulatory guidance relevant to producing and broadcasting Video News Releases (VNRs) — video segments that resemble news reports but are produced by PR/marketing entities. Covers production techniques, disclosure expectations, broadcaster practices, and U.S. legal scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / origin of VNR
rubrics_metrics.description: A video segment made to look like a news report, but is instead created by a PR firm, advertising agency, marketing firm, corporation, government agency, or non-profit organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition to classify content as a VNR (i.e., produced for promotional/publicity purposes rather than by independent newsroom staff). This distinction underlies subsequent ethical and legal expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure/Identification of source
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics of VNRs have called the practice deceptive or a propaganda technique, particularly when the segment is not identified to the viewers as a VNR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice / legal expectation (per FCC guidance) is to disclose that material was produced by a government agency or PR/marketing entity. Non-disclosure is an anti-pattern and has drawn regulatory warnings and fines in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of on-air reporters or actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Most VNRs feature a professional news reporter, someone with on-air news experience, or an actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a person who appears to be a reporter (real or actor) increases the risk of misleading viewers; government-produced VNRs that used an on-screen 'reporter' were found by the GAO to violate law in some cases (e.g., the 'Karen Ryan' videos).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and treatment of interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: VNRs often include interviews with experts (who often have legitimate, if biased, expertise); so called 'man on the street' interviews with 'average' people; and pictures of celebrities, products, service demonstrations, corporate logos and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews may be spontaneously conducted or actors may be hired and directed to deliver scripted comments. Producers frequently excerpt and edit interviews into 'sound bites' that support the intended message — an editorial technique that can mislead if origins/selection are not transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing discretion / sound-bite construction
rubrics_metrics.description: VNR producers and directors, just like journalists, have complete discretion to excerpt and edit these 'interviews' into 'sound bites' that help make the point they are trying to make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awareness of selective editing is crucial for newsrooms: editing choices shape narrative and can produce misleading impressions if context or source is not disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcaster editorial discretion and modification
rubrics_metrics.description: News producers may air VNRs, in whole or in part, at their discretion or incorporate them into news reports if they contain information appropriate to a story or of interest to viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stations often broadcast only portions of a VNR; sometimes they use the script provided by the VNR producer but frequently they write their own script. Ethical practice calls for evaluating VNR content the same as any external material and disclosing provenance when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of disguise / passing VNRs as original reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports (e.g., Center for Media and Democracy) have alleged that television stations actively disguised VNR content to make it appear to be their own reporting; more than one-third of the time, stations aired the pre-packaged VNR in its entirety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disguising externally produced content as internal reporting is an anti-pattern; stations should avoid presenting prepackaged material as their own without clear attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and intended uses of VNRs
rubrics_metrics.description: They are provided to television newsrooms to shape public opinion, promote commercial products and services, publicize individuals, or support other interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the promotional intent (equivalent of a press release in video form per PRSA). This purpose affects how newsrooms should vet and present the material to audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR industry framing (PRSA position)
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the trade-group Public Relations Society of America, a VNR is the video equivalent of a press release and presents a client's case in an attractive, informative format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR practitioners view VNRs as marketing/communication tools; producers emphasize that editorial judgement remains with journalists/program producers, but this claim does not remove disclosure or ethical obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical practice: tracking and encoding
rubrics_metrics.description: Public Relations agencies have their video tapes encoded allowing very accurate tracking of where such video is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encoding/trackable feeds are common production practices used to monitor placement and distribution; broadcasters and regulators may use this information when investigating use of VNR material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/regulatory scrutiny and FCC guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Communications Commission warned television stations that they could be fined for airing news stories provided by the government and by companies without disclosing who made them, and in 2006 ordered a review and sent letters to stations asking about agreements with VNR creators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcasters should be aware of FCC warnings and inquiries. Failing to disclose the source of prepackaged material, or receiving 'consideration' for airing it without disclosure, can trigger regulatory action.

rubrics_metrics.name: GAO rulings on government-produced VNRs
rubrics_metrics.description: GAO decisions concluded that Department of Health and Human Services and Department of Education VNRs using an on-screen 'reporter' were in violation of federal law (e.g., Karen Ryan video rulings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government agencies producing VNRs must comply with legal restrictions; using prepackaged video that presents as independent journalism can constitute unlawful propaganda or improper use of public funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/statutory context (Smith–Mundt and proposed legislation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Smith–Mundt Act of 1948 governed U.S. information activities overseas; separate proposals such as the 'Stop Government Propaganda Act' have been introduced to address government-produced propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand statutory background when evaluating government-produced VNRs; policy and law evolution affects permissible government communications domestically and internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of problematic uses (case studies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances cited include local stations airing a Department of Health and Human Services video presenting the Medicare plan as conventional journalism and Amazon-produced PR pieces where anchors read an identical script verbatim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cited examples as cautionary case studies when crafting newsroom policies: identical scripts across stations and government-produced videos that mimic reporting are red flags for lack of transparency.
